articles.title: Konecranes reports strong port equipment deliveries despite order slowdown
articles.summary: Finnish lifting equipment manufacturer Konecranes reported a strong recovery in port equipment deliveries during the third quarter of 2026, although new orders in its Port Solutions business declined significantly compared with the previous year. According to its interim financial report published on October 23, the...
articles.body: Finnish lifting equipment manufacturer Konecranes reported a strong recovery in port equipment deliveries during the third quarter of 2026, although new orders in its Port Solutions business declined significantly compared with the previous year. According to its interim financial report published on October 23, the company’s Port Solutions division recorded net sales of €420 million during July–September, representing an increase of 28.3% in comparable currencies. However, order intake in the division declined by 36.7% in comparable currencies to €288 million, reflecting volatility in the timing of customer orders. Despite the decline in new orders, the division’s comparable EBITA margin improved to 12.0%, compared with 11.8% in the corresponding period of 2025, supported primarily by higher delivery volumes. Konecranes said customer activity remained strong across its port equipment product lines, while the timing of new orders was unfavourable during the quarter. Port equipment deliveries support quarterly performance The contrasting performance between orders and sales highlights the impact of project timing on the company’s port equipment business. While Port Solutions experienced a significant reduction in quarterly order intake, deliveries accelerated, contributing to stronger revenue and improved profitability. CEO Marko Tulokas said the company’s third-quarter performance benefited from solid delivery execution, particularly within Port Solutions. The company also indicated that its Port Solutions order book remained approximately at the same level as a year earlier, despite the decline in quarterly orders. At group level, Konecranes reported third-quarter net sales of €1.10 billion, up 11.4% year-on-year, while total order intake decreased by 12.0% to €1.01 billion. Comparable EBITA increased to €172.2 million from €164.9 million, although the corresponding margin declined to 15.6% from 16.7%. For the first nine months of 2026, the group’s order intake reached €3.32 billion, while its order book increased by 8.0% to €3.30 billion. Container handling outlook remains positive Looking ahead, Konecranes maintained a positive long-term assessment of container handling activity, despite ongoing uncertainty surrounding international trade and geopolitical developments. The company noted that container throughput remained at elevated levels, supporting the longer-term prospects for demand in port equipment and container handling. However, Konecranes acknowledged that geopolitical uncertainty and trade policy tensions continued to affect the operating environment. The company reiterated its full-year 2026 financial guidance, expecting net sales to remain approximately unchanged or increase compared with 2025. It also expects its comparable EBITA margin to remain approximately at the previous year’s level. The results come as Konecranes continues implementing its updated strategy, announced in September, focusing on profitable growth, technological development and expanding its presence across existing business areas. For port operators, the company’s latest results indicate continued equipment deliveries and an active customer pipeline, although the timing of new investment commitments remains uneven.

articles.title: CEVA Logistics and Zalando advance AI-powered warehouse robotics
articles.summary: CEVA Logistics and Zalando are collaborating with Sereact, NVIDIA and Nebius on an artificial intelligence training system designed to improve robotic handling of e-commerce returns and accelerate the development of automated warehouse operations. Announced on October 22, 2026, the initiative introduces a closed-loop...
articles.body: CEVA Logistics and Zalando are collaborating with Sereact, NVIDIA and Nebius on an artificial intelligence training system designed to improve robotic handling of e-commerce returns and accelerate the development of automated warehouse operations. Announced on October 22, 2026, the initiative introduces a closed-loop training process for Cortex, Sereact’s robotic AI system, combining real-world warehouse data with simulation, model training and performance evaluation. The initial deployment targets Zalando’s returns handling operations at selected CEVA Logistics fulfillment centers, where robotic systems must process products arriving in varying conditions, packaging formats and configurations. According to the companies, the new approach is designed to shorten robotic training and improvement cycles from weeks to days, allowing systems to adapt more quickly to changing product assortments and operational requirements. AI simulation accelerates robotic training The system combines Sereact’s Cortex vision-language-action model with NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab and Cosmos technologies, supported by Nebius’ Physical AI Workbench. During warehouse operations, Sereact’s robotic stations collect data from actual returns handling activities, including video recordings and robotic movement information. These datasets are transferred to Nebius’ cloud infrastructure, where NVIDIA Isaac Lab generates simulated variations of real-world handling scenarios. NVIDIA Cosmos then produces additional variations involving different garment conditions, packaging materials and lighting environments. The expanded datasets are used to further train Cortex on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, enabling the robotic system to encounter a wider range of potential handling situations before updated software is tested in operational environments. Each updated policy is evaluated against predefined performance criteria established by Sereact. Successful versions proceed to real-world testing, while those that fail trigger additional simulation and training focused on the identified weaknesses. The process is coordinated through an AI agent using NVIDIA’s Physical AI Data Factory skills and Nebius’ Workbench framework. Engineers establish training objectives and approve operations exceeding predefined computing cost limits. Targeting complex e-commerce returns operations Returns handling presents particular challenges for warehouse automation because products can arrive folded, crumpled, unpackaged or without their original labels. Robotic systems must identify, pick, inspect and sort these items while adapting to changing product ranges and seasonal demand. Within the partnership, Sereact provides its Cortex AI model and dual-arm robotic returns stations, while NVIDIA supplies simulation and training technologies. Nebius provides the cloud infrastructure and development environment through its European data centers. CEVA Logistics hosts the robotic stations within its fulfillment operations for Zalando, which supplies the returns-handling use case for evaluating the technology. The companies aim to create a continuous improvement process in which data collected during warehouse operations can be used to develop and test updated robotic capabilities more efficiently. Beyond the initial logistics application, the closed-loop training pipeline is available as a reference architecture through Nebius’ Physical AI Workbench. The framework includes NVIDIA’s Physical AI Data Factory skills and is accessible to robotics development teams using Nebius AI Cloud, with computing and storage resources charged according to usage. The collaboration highlights efforts to integrate physical AI, cloud computing and robotic automation into complex fulfillment operations, particularly processes that require systems to adapt to unpredictable product conditions.

articles.title: Rhenus launches major automated warehouse system in Poland
articles.summary: Rhenus Warehousing Solutions has officially launched one of Poland’s largest AutoStore installations at its logistics centre in Bolesławiec, strengthening its automated warehousing capabilities and expanding support for e-commerce operations. The system, inaugurated on October 22, 2026, is the second-largest...
articles.body: Rhenus Warehousing Solutions has officially launched one of Poland’s largest AutoStore installations at its logistics centre in Bolesławiec, strengthening its automated warehousing capabilities and expanding support for e-commerce operations. The system, inaugurated on October 22, 2026, is the second-largest AutoStore installation within the Rhenus Group. It occupies 4,500 square metres inside the company’s 57,000-square-metre logistics facility. Designed to improve storage efficiency and order fulfillment, the installation uses more than 100 autonomous robots operating across a grid-based storage system containing nearly 140,000 bins. It has the capacity to accommodate approximately 1.8 million product units and can handle more than 38,000 bin presentations per day. The project forms part of Rhenus’ broader European warehouse automation strategy, aimed at supporting the growing operational requirements of e-commerce customers. Automation strengthens warehouse operations The installation was implemented by Element Logic, an automated warehouse solutions provider, following an eight-month implementation process. Preparatory work began in late 2025, while the main installation phase took place between March and July 2026. The project also involved system testing and adaptations to the warehouse management system (WMS). According to Rhenus, the new AutoStore system has already tripled the efficiency of the processes it supports, although the company did not provide further details on the measurement. The installation also incorporates the largest bins available for the AutoStore system, allowing the facility to accommodate a broader range of products, including larger items. “Implementation of the AutoStore system at our own facility in Bolesławiec marks another milestone in the development of the operations in Poland,” said Paweł Nowak, Country Manager, Rhenus Warehousing Solutions Poland. He added that the technology would support higher operational efficiency and the continued development of automated warehouse logistics. Supporting e-commerce growth in Europe The investment builds on Rhenus’ experience with automated storage and order-picking technologies across its European network. The company introduced its first AutoStore installation in the Netherlands in 2018 and has since expanded its use of automated warehousing solutions. The Bolesławiec project is designed to improve picking speed and accuracy while increasing storage density and operational scalability. “Our customers expect speed, flexibility and scalability. The AutoStore enables us to meet these expectations while creating a future-ready logistics operation that can continue to grow alongside our customers’ businesses,” said Ronny Sassen, CEO of Rhenus Contract Logistics. Rhenus expects the installation to support the development of its warehousing activities in Poland while providing additional capacity to meet changing e-commerce fulfillment requirements.

articles.title: Tankers: More Complications Ahead for Diesel Cargoes?
articles.summary: The diesel trade seems to be somewhat reopening, with Russian volumes starting to make their way across the Atlantic, but complications remain, with availability more than limited. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “the Trump administration has been busy easing sanctions over the past couple of...
articles.body: Tankers: More Complications Ahead for Diesel Cargoes? in Hellenic Shipping News 26/10/2026 T he diesel trade seems to be somewhat reopening, with Russian volumes starting to make their way across the Atlantic, but complications remain, with availability more than limited. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “the Trump administration has been busy easing sanctions over the past couple of weeks. On 9 October, OFAC issued General License 135. It allows the sale, delivery and import into the US of Russian-origin diesel until 7 April 2027. On 16 October, Trump waived the main measures of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed on 18 September. The Act provides for a 500% tariff on Russian goods and up to 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. Last week, news also emerged that the administration was considering easing shadow fleet sanctions, as covered in last week’s report”. According to Gibson, “of the three measures, the Graham Act waiver has no physical impact, as the tariffs were never in force. Easing shadow fleet sanctions could, to an extent, provide some additional tanker capacity, primarily for shuttle runs through Hormuz. The diesel licence sits somewhere in between: it is unlikely to meaningfully ease the global diesel shortage, but it carries a strong political message”. Gibson commented that “the first problem with the diesel waiver is volume, as Russia has little to spare. Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries cut domestic supply, prompting Moscow to ban diesel exports in July. Seaborne exports from western terminals fell to an average of 510kt per month in Q3, from 3.27mt per month last year. Following the agreement with the US, the Russian government has begun lifting the restrictions, authorising the immediate release of 500kt for export globally. It has also confirmed it stands ready to supply 300kt to the US this month, followed by 500kt in November and 1mt in December, with three MRs reportedly already heading to the US with diesel. So far, however, preliminary trade data shows little change, with October exports to date only modestly above levels seen over the July-September period. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes continue. The Ryazan refinery was hit again on 15 October, and Russian officials reported another attack on a refinery in the St Petersburg area on 18 October. Still, Kyiv has shown some willingness to compromise: on 19 October, President Zelensky offered a 30-day pause in return for Patriot cover for Ukraine’s airspace. Washington has not signalled it will accept, and instead pressed Kyiv to halt strikes altogether”. Source: Gibson Shipbrokers Ltd Meanwhile, the shipbroker added that “the legal side is another stumbling block. The licence does not cover sanctioned vessels, services such as bunkering, or the price cap, which limits the role of mainstream tankers. EU and UK rules have not changed either. The EU still bans trading, brokering and transporting Russian diesel unless it is within the price cap. EU and UK banks and insurers cannot finance or insure cargoes above the cap, and with diesel prices this high, many cargoes are likely to be above it. In the US, the licence may also face a legal challenge, since the 2022 Russian oil import ban can only be lifted once the President certifies to Congress that its conditions have been met”. “In the near term, volumes are unlikely to amount to anything meaningful unless attacks on Russian refineries stop. However, if Ukraine is successfully pressed to halt the attacks, the implications would be considerably bigger, as that would eventually allow Russia to export more to its usual trading partners, not just the US. Politically, Trump appears to be warming to Russia, although his position can change quickly. With this shift in Washington and parts of Europe grappling with social unrest amidst mass migration, rising living costs, soaring fuel prices and the growing influence of right-wing political parties, could Europe be forced to also reconsider its position?”, Gibson concluded Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: XENETA: Far East to Europe spot rates rise despite Red Sea return as demand overrides supply in International Shipping News 26/10/2026 The Xeneta Weekly Ocean Container Shipping Market Update provides data and intelligence including the latest freight rate and capacity movements across global trades with supporting insight from Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst. Xeneta analyst insight – Far East to Europe spot rates rise despite Red Sea return as demand overrides supply Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst: “Despite the continuing return of container shipping services to the Red Sea freeing up capacity in the fleet, spot rates from the Far East to North Europe and Mediterranean are up 6.8% and 5.8% respectively from a week ago. This follows steady decline since July before spot rates reached an invisible floor last week and are now starting an upward trend. “This is a conundrum because the release of capacity into the global fleet should ease pressure on rates, but we are seeing the opposite. Spot rates are still up 67% into North Europe and 33% into Mediterranean compared to pre-Hormuz crisis on 28 February. “Part of the answer to the conundrum of rates holding up in the face of increasing capacity is found in strong demand on these lanes, with volumes shipped from Far East to Europe up 12.2% in the first seven months of the year. “Disruption such as Middle East conflict brings volatility and sudden shocks, but demand is a powerful upward force for rates. If demand is not there, then rates will collapse, but it has been strong enough on the European fronthauls to prevent this, even as Red Sea capacity returns. “Spot rates from the Far East to the US West Coast and US East Coast are essentially flat from a week ago, up 0.2% on both trades. This confirms the US trades have peaked and we expect them to soften through the remainder of 2026. “Spot rates into the US East Coast remain more than three times those into North Europe.” Data highlights Market average spot rates – 23 October 2026: Far East to US West Coast: USD 8,311 per FEU (40ft container) Far East to US East Coast: USD 11,525 per FEU Far East to North Europe: USD 3,698 per FEU Far East to Mediterranean: USD 4,442 per FEU North Europe to US East Coast: USD 2,963 per FEU Change from a week ago (since 16 Oct 2026): Far East to US West Coast: +0.2% Far East to US East Coast: +0.2% Far East to North Europe: +6.8% Far East to Mediterranean: +5.8% North Europe to US East Coast: -0.2% Change since 1 July 2026: Far East to US West Coast: +18.9% Far East to US East Coast: +31.7% Far East to North Europe: -33.2% Far East to Mediterranean: -36.7% North Europe to US East Coast: +16.0% Change since pre-Hormuz crisis (28 Feb 2026): Far East to US West Coast: +342% Far East to US East Coast: +335% Far East to North Europe: +67% Far East to Mediterranean: +33% North Europe to US East Coast: +101% Source: XENETA 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Capesize Market Recovering Steadily in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 26/10/2026 C apesize The Capesize market recovered steadily through the week, with improving sentiment across both basins lifting the BCI 182 5TC from $30,518 on Monday to $34,380 by Friday. The Pacific led the initial recovery, supported by renewed operator demand, increased miner participation and talk of potential weather-related delays in China. C5 rates advanced from the low $12s to the $14.15–14.25 range by midweek. While activity eased towards Thursday, underlying support remained evident, with miners continuing to cover early-November requirements. The South Brazil and West Africa to China markets also gathered momentum, with C3 rates advancing from the low $31s to the $34.00–34.50 range as bids for forward dates moved progressively higher amid limited offers. However, towards the close of the week, rumours of a $33.25 fixture for 15–20 November weighed on sentiment. Demand became increasingly concentrated on end-November and some November–December split dates. In contrast, the North Atlantic remained comparatively subdued, with limited transatlantic enquiry and a slight softening towards the end of the week, despite earlier activity on the Fronthaul route. Panamax-Kamsarmax The week was characterised by persistent downward pressure across both basins, with the P5TC declining consistently as the week progressed. The Atlantic remained the weaker region by a significant margin, as limited cargo replenishment, subdued grain and mineral demand, and an oversupply of tonnage continued to favour charterers. Reflecting these conditions, an 82,000-dwt open in the North Continent fixed a transatlantic round at $22,500, while a 75,000-dwt secured a similar trip basis delivery East Coast South America at $33,000. Transatlantic activity steadily lost momentum, while fronthaul business came under increasing pressure as owners repeatedly reduced expectations to secure employment. A 93,000-dwt fixed a US East Coast trip to India basis delivery passing Gibraltar at $31,000. Conditions in East Coast South America were particularly challenging, with abundant vessel availability and insufficient enquiry weighing heavily on rates. An 82,000-dwt fixed basis delivery Singapore for an East Coast South America fronthaul at $21,000 early in the week, although levels deteriorated noticeably as the week progressed. The Pacific proved comparatively more resilient throughout the week. Healthy demand from Australia and broadly balanced conditions in Indonesia helped underpin sentiment, although North Pacific activity was more subdued. An 85,000-dwt fixed an East Coast Australia round at $24,000, while an 82,000-dwt secured a similar run at comparable levels. Elsewhere, an 85,000-dwt fixed a North Pacific round voyage at $26,000, while a 76,000-dwt fixed a short Indonesia trip at $21,500. Ultramax/Supramax A week of rather muted activity, however the index finished the week above last week’s close. Rates in the US Gulf softened as new enquiries were insufficient to satisfy a lengthening tonnage list, with rates varying during the week from $34,000 to $31,000 for a 64,000-dwt from US Gulf to the West Mediterranean with grains and longer trips to the Far East below these levels. The south fared slightly better due to limited availability, but was lacking much direction, whilst the Continent and Mediterranean markets had quiet weeks. Asia was again the main driver, although NoPac grain trades slowed, the backhaul market took up the slack and rates climbed with a 63,000-dwt fixed from North China to West Africa at $27,500 and a 55,000-dwt fixed for clinker from North China to Chittagong at a strong $32,000. Due to the continued firm spot market, Operators were keen to take period tonnage to cover backhauls, with a 64,000-dwt open Busan fixed for minimum 4 to about 6 months at $24,250. Handysize The market strengthened modestly over the week. The South Atlantic was the strongest region, supported by healthy demand and tight prompt tonnage. Reported fixtures included a 38,000-dwt open Santos on 30 October, placed on subjects for a trip from Recalada to the West Coast of South America at $36,000. Meanwhile, the Continent and Mediterranean remained broadly balanced around last-done levels. A 39,000-dwt was fixed for a trip from Antwerp to the US Gulf at $19,500. The US Gulf remained under pressure, as limited demand struggled to absorb a growing tonnage list. A 40,000-dwt open Houston on 21 October was fixed for a trip from Dos Bocas to India with petcoke at $19,000. The Pacific was generally positive despite periods of limited activity, with tight tonnage supporting firm backhaul and round-trip rates. A 40,000-dwt open CJK spot was fixed for a trip to the East Coast of India at $22,000. Period activity was also evident, highlighted by a 37,000-dwt fixed from Recalada for five to seven months, with worldwide redelivery, at $19,500. articles.title: Testing fleet strategies against an uncertain energy transition
articles.summary: Balancing transition risk and cost is central to developing robust fuel and technology strategies for the journey towards 2050. This year’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 outlines DNV’s framework for evaluating these trade-offs across both short- and long-term horizons and demonstrates its use through a case study of very...
articles.body: Testing fleet strategies against an uncertain energy transition in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 26/10/2026 B alancing transition risk and cost is central to developing robust fuel and technology strategies for the journey towards 2050. This year’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 outlines DNV’s framework for evaluating these trade-offs across both short- and long-term horizons and demonstrates its use through a case study of very large crude carriers. The scenario-based framework supports the assessment of transition risk and the identification of fuel and technology pathways that balance cost and risk at fleet level. The analysis shows that fleet strategies can perform very differently depending on how the energy transition unfolds, with markedly different outcomes across the defined slow- and rapid-transition scenarios. “The case study also highlights how the cost and risk assessment outputs can be combined into an overall strategy score for more robust decision-making,” says Øyvind Sekkesæter, Senior Consultant at DNV and lead author of this year’s Maritime Forecast report. Updating the framework for managing energy transition risk The case study involves an updated version of DNV’s three-step framework for integrating qualitative, non-monetary risks with financial modelling. Step 1 defines potential fleet strategies, including outlining fuel choices, retrofits, and fleet renewal. Step 2 defines scenarios and involves modelling regulatory timelines, fuel availability, and pricing. Step 3 conducts robustness checks by stress-testing strategies against scenarios with respect to both risk and cost. Case study: A VLCC fleet for renewal Maritime Forecast to 2050 applies the framework to a shipowner managing five very large crude carriers (VLCCs) trading on the spot market with limited EU/EEA exposure. The fleet consists of conventional, scrubber-fitted vessels without shore power capability: two built in 2010, one in 2015, and two in 2020. A structured fleet renewal programme replaces each vessel at 20 years of age, starting in 2030. Defining the strategies The case study compares two potential fleet strategies from 2026 to 2050. Strategy A: HSHFO + scrubber (illustrated below) – here, the owner continues ordering conventional-fuel newbuilds with open-loop scrubbers to exploit cheap high sulphur heavy fuel oil (HSHFO). The existing fleet utilizes basic operational measures (hull cleaning, weather routing) without physical retrofits. Strategy B: Phase-in of dual-fuel LNG ships – here, the owner transitions to LNG dual-fuel newbuilds designed with advanced energy efficiency (shaft generators) and shore power. In 2026, the three newest existing ships undergo retrofits. These install pre- and post-swirl energy-saving devices, variable-frequency drives on seawater pumps, and low-friction silicone hull coatings. Two potential transition scenarios are defined for stress-testing the strategies. Assessing costs by strategy and scenario The cost assessment in the study signals a widening gap between the two scenarios when it comes to break-even daily rates up to 2049. Cost performance, reflecting capital, operations, fuel, and compliance expenses, determines the average break-even daily rate per ship. Both strategies start with break-even rates of approximately USD 52,000/day in 2026. In the slow transition scenario, Strategy A remains the lower-cost choice, rising to approximately USD 61,000/day by 2049. Strategy B is penalized by the higher capital cost of dual-fuel LNG newbuilds, reaching approximately USD 67,000/day. In the rapid transition scenario, the economic balance is reversed. Strategy A’s break-even rate soars to approximately USD 167,000/day by 2049 due to high compliance penalties and expensive low-GHG diesel. Strategy B’s break-even rate rises to a lower rate of approximately USD 144,000/day, benefiting from lower fuel consumption and cheaper low-GHG methane. Risk assessment and scoring The risk assessment, structured as a Hazard Identification (HAZID), maps events across a 1–3 probability and consequence scale. In the rapid transition scenario, Strategy A faces high-risk events (represented by higher scores), such as the inability to bunker sufficient low-GHG diesel, or encountering localized port bans on open-loop scrubbers. Full tables of the HAZID assessment are provided in the paper. “To mitigate risks such as insufficient access to low-GHG diesel, shipowners can implement compliance pooling, enter into long-term fuel offtake agreements, or contractually transfer compliance liabilities to charterers,” Sekkesæter comments. In the slow transition scenario, both strategies share similar risk scores, but Strategy B has a cost score. Under the rapid transition scenario, Strategy A performs significantly worse on both dimensions, while Strategy B proves more resilient across cost and risk metrics. Cost and risk assessment outputs can also be combined into an overall strategy score in several ways that allow direct comparison of alternative fuel and technology pathways. Scenario likelihoods can be weighted in the framework to reflect different views on the future. For example, if rapid transition is judged more likely than slow transition, the overall score would give more weight to the rapid scenario scores. “The case study shows how this framework supports the structured comparison of fleet strategies and makes explicit the trade-offs between cost efficiency and exposure to transition risk. The overall score provides a relative measure of a strategy’s robustness across different transition scenarios,” Sekkesæter concludes. Source: DNV, https://www.dnv.com/expert-story/maritime-impact/testing-fleet-strategies-against-an-uncertain-energy-transition/ Tops 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: This year’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 outlines DNV’s framework for evaluating these trade-offs across both short- and long-term horizons and demonstrates its use through a case study of very large crude carriers.
The scenario-based framework supports the assessment of transition risk and the identification of fuel and technology pathways that balance cost and risk at fleet level.

The analysis shows that fleet strategies can perform very differently depending on how the energy transition unfolds, with markedly different outcomes across the defined slow- and rapid-transition scenarios.

articles.body: Russian diesel tanker heads to New York as Kremlin claims regular shipments in International Shipping News 26/10/2026 The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes is heading to New York carrying Russian diesel, according to S&P Global Energy Commodities at Sea data, with the Kremlin expecting deliveries to continue “on a regular basis.” The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Oct. 23 that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was sent to the US. “The first tanker has, in fact, set off toward its destinations — to its buyers — and [subsequent shipments] will continue on a regular basis,” Peskov told journalists, according to TASS. He did not clarify the name of the vessel sent to the US or who the buyers of the delivery are. The Agioi Fanendes tanker left Russia’s port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and is expected to reach New York around Nov. 6-7, according to CAS data. It is unclear who the buyer and the seller of the vessel might be. The first diesel tanker from Russia to the US since 2022 is expected to carry about 40,000 metric tons, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Oct. 21. Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, which manages the Agioi Fanendes, according to its website, could not be reached for comment Oct. 23. Zelenskyy said Oct. 15 that US military officials told their counterparts that if Ukraine did not stop the energy strikes, the US would block intelligence sharing with Ukraine. articles.body: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: Lower feedstock costs limit Rotterdam B30-VLSFO price gain in International Shipping News 26/10/2026 Europe Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has gained $11/mt in the past week, while the Dutch port’s conventional VLSFO price has jumped $30/mt over the same period. This has narrowed Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $19/mt, to $155/mt. Dutch suppliers can generate ZRE A tickets for selling low-carbon fuels, which can be traded with other suppliers. The price of these tickets held at €240/mtCO2e ($269/mtCO2e) on Thursday this week, unchanged from last Thursday. These ZRE A tickets help lower Rotterdam’s biofuel prices compared with other ports. Belgium has no such mechanism. Prima Markets’ ARA UCOME and POMEME barge prices, both indicators of feedstock sourcing costs, have each dropped $73/mt in the past week, to $1,682/mt and $1,752/mt respectively. That leaves UCOME at a $70/mt discount to POMEME. Lower feedstock costs may have helped narrow Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO premium over conventional VLSFO. Rotterdam’s bio-bunker demand has also weakened. Suppliers in the port sold 154,000 mt of bio-bunker fuel in the third quarter, down 38% from the second quarter, Port of Rotterdam data shows. Bio-VLSFO sales more than halved to 63,000 mt, while bio-MGO sales slipped just 4% to 41,000 mt. The port authority does not report B100 separately and says it is most probably included in bio-MGO. B100 samples recorded by ENGINE in Rotterdam more than doubled in the first eight months of the year, and growing B100 demand may help explain why bio-MGO sales held steady. In the neighbouring Belgian port of Antwerp, B100 (UCOME) has been priced at $1,974/mt today, down $10/mt on the week. Antwerp-Bruges’ biofuel bunker sales halved from the previous quarter to 13,000 mt in the third quarter, port authority data shows. That was the port’s lowest quarterly biofuel volume since the fourth quarter of last year. Biofuels made up less than 1% of the port’s total bunker sales of 2.16 million mt in the third quarter. Gibraltar’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) is priced at $1,050/mt, a $252/mt premium over the port’s conventional VLSFO price. Asia Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has dropped $22/mt in the past week to $1,128/mt, even as the port’s conventional VLSFO price has gained $35/mt over the same period. This has narrowed Singapore’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $57/mt, to $184/mt. Prima Markets’ price assessment for China UCOME cargo, which is a key feedstock for Singapore’s B30-VLSFO blend, has held at $1,220/mt, unchanged from last week. B100 has been priced at $1,493/mt in Singapore today. Source: By Nachiket Tekawade, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: EU Proposed SMAP subsidy favors e-fuels and bioLNG
articles.summary: Europe’s carbon market could soon start paying shipowners to switch fuels, but the support on offer is far from equal. articles.body: EU Proposed SMAP subsidy favors e-fuels and bioLNG in International Shipping News 26/10/2026 Europe’s carbon market could soon start paying shipowners to switch fuels, but the support on offer is far from equal. In July, the European Commission proposed a revision of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) that would reserve up to 110 million allowances between 2028 and 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, which is meant to cover part of the price gap between fossil marine fuels and sustainable alternatives. Rystad Energy’s analysis shows that, combined with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would reshape the cost ranking of marine fuels in Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels stand to gain the most, while biodiesel made from used cooking oil (UCO) and animal fats – one of today’s most widely used marine biofuels – is left out. The timing matters. From 2026, shipping companies surrender ETS allowances for 100% of their verified emissions in scope, now including methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime requires a steadily tightening cut in the greenhouse-gas intensity of energy used on board. Both regimes rest on the sustainability rules of the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III). For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the question is which fuel pathway the combined rules reward. SMAP would cover 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with 10 additional percentage points where the feedstock is sourced in the EU. Because support scales with the size of the gap, the most expensive fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could see its entire remaining premium covered (Figure 1). Support is halved on voyages into or out of the EU, and fuels generally must be produced in the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market. Stacked together, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO) on intra-EU voyages. At 3Q26 prices, bioLNG costs more than twice as much as VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at about half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are counted. Most of that advantage comes from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Because bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas (LNG) engines, this strengthens the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. RFNBOs receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few ships can burn ammonia today and EU production remains small. The clearest losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. UCO and category 1 and 2 animal fats meet every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP supports only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of RED III. Biogas, by contrast, appears eligible regardless of feedstock. The exclusion matters because of how Europe’s biodiesel industry is built. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as UCO and other waste fats and oils are expected to account for about 96% of the region’s biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support (Figure 2). Aviation’s sustainable fuel mandate is drawing on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel. Even for eligible fuels, SMAP is more likely to steer early movers than to drive large volumes. The budget is fixed at around $900 million per year if spread evenly, and claims are cut pro rata when oversubscribed, so owners learn the support per tonne only after the year ends. For bioLNG, mass balance rules also limit supply to bunkers from grid-connected liquefaction in the EU. The proposal still faces negotiation with the European Parliament and European Council, and the final rules could narrow eligibility or curb overcompensation. Nonetheless, the direction for shipowners is clear: in European trades, fuels that perform well under the ETS, FuelEU Maritime and SMAP together are likely to win. Owners with LNG dual-fuel tonnage and early movers in e-fuels stand to benefit most, while those relying on waste-oil biodiesel should prepare for a widening cost gap. This relative stability is reflected on most lanes, indicating that, with few exceptions, carriers extended rates for the first fortnight into the second. • Spot rates from Greater China to Northeast, Southeast and South Asia remained mostly stable this week except on the Shanghai–Busan and Shanghai–Kaohsiung routes. Rates from Shanghai to Busan rose 14% to $1,135 per 40ft container, while those to Kaohsiung increased 8% to $1,313 per 40ft container. Average vessel waiting times increased in Week 42 at Busan and Singapore, rising from 23 to 31 hours and from 10 to 12 hours, respectively. Meanwhile, the Golden Week provided an opportunity for ports to clear backlogs and improve schedule reliability, supported by reduced cargo volumes and blank sailings. Average vessel waiting times declined in Week 42 at Shanghai, Ningbo and Tanjung Pelepas, falling from 58 to 38 hours, 40 to 34 hours and 34 to 21 hours, respectively. The deteriorating situation in the Middle East kept Shanghai–Jebel Ali rates elevated at $8,451 per 40ft container. Drewry expects rates to remain broadly stable in the coming weeks, but further capacity additions could put upwards pressure on supply and threaten market stability. • Spot rates on trade routes across Southeast and Northeast Asia remained mostly stable except for routes originating from Busan and Ho Chi Minh City. Rates from Busan to Shanghai increased 11% to $176 per 40ft container, while rates from Ho Chi Minh City to Shanghai decreased 6% to $44 per 40ft container. Pacific International Lines (PIL) is set to launch its new JKS service on 5 November to strengthen its Straits–Indonesia network. The two-week service will deploy two vessels of 1,900–2,600 teu, calling at Singapore, Laem Chabang and Jakarta. Drewry expects freight rates to stabilise in the coming weeks. • The intra-Asia container freight market has remained resilient this year, with the index surging 188% YoY. High bunker costs and ongoing US–Iran tensions continued to push up rates, with Brent crude prices remaining around $100 per barrel since early October, adding to carriers’ operating costs. Meanwhile, congestion eased at key ports during Golden Week as reduced cargo volumes and blank sailings helped clear backlog and improved schedule reliability. articles.summary: Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG (HHLA) has lowered its earnings forecast for the 2026 financial year, citing strike-related disruptions, challenges associated with the ramp-up of terminal automation in Hamburg and a non-cash impairment charge in its Logistics segment. The German port and logistics operator now...
articles.body: Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG (HHLA) has lowered its earnings forecast for the 2026 financial year, citing strike-related disruptions, challenges associated with the ramp-up of terminal automation in Hamburg and a non-cash impairment charge in its Logistics segment. The German port and logistics operator now expects Group operating profit (EBIT) of between €115 million and €135 million, down from its previous forecast of €150 million to €170 million. The revision follows weaker-than-expected container throughput at HHLA’s Hamburg terminals, where industrial action and the ongoing implementation of additional automation have affected operational performance. HHLA has also revised its container throughput outlook and now anticipates a significant year-on-year decline in 2026, compared with its previous expectation of a slight decrease. Port logistics earnings under pressure For its Port Logistics subgroup, HHLA has reduced its full-year EBIT forecast to between €100 million and €120 million, compared with the previously projected range of €135 million to €155 million. According to the company, strike-related disruptions and the ramp-up phase of further automation at its Hamburg container terminals have contributed to container handling volumes falling below expectations, placing additional pressure on earnings. The revised guidance reflects the company’s assessment of business performance to date and updated estimates for the final quarter of 2026. Alongside these operational challenges, HHLA has reviewed its portfolio of equity investments in new and spin-off business activities as part of its strategic focus on core operations. Following market assessments, the company identified a non-cash impairment loss of approximately €12 million in its Logistics segment, which also contributes to the downward revision of its earnings expectations. Revenue and container transport outlook unchanged Despite the reduced profitability forecast and weaker container throughput expectations, HHLA has maintained its existing guidance for revenue and container transport. The company continues to anticipate a significant increase in revenue for the 2026 financial year, while container transport volumes are expected to record a slight year-on-year increase. The unchanged forecasts highlight the different developments across HHLA’s operations, with weaker container handling activity at its Hamburg terminals contrasting with its expectations for revenue and container transport. The revised outlook places particular attention on the operational performance of HHLA’s container terminals during the remainder of 2026, as the company continues the ramp-up of further automation while managing the effects of earlier disruptions.

articles.title: ID Logistics inaugurates automated logistics hub for PUMA in France
articles.summary: ID Logistics and sportswear company PUMA have officially inaugurated an automated logistics facility in Vendenheim, France, marking a new milestone in their ten-year partnership and strengthening PUMA’s distribution operations in the French market. The 41,000-square-metre facility, developed by LCR – Les...
articles.body: ID Logistics and sportswear company PUMA have officially inaugurated an automated logistics facility in Vendenheim, France, marking a new milestone in their ten-year partnership and strengthening PUMA’s distribution operations in the French market. The 41,000-square-metre facility, developed by LCR – Les Constructeurs Réunis, is dedicated to PUMA’s business-to-business (B2B) operations. Although officially inaugurated on October 21, 2026, the site has been operational since late 2025, following the transfer of logistics activities from Landersheim. The facility is designed to process up to 57,000 order lines per day, with a target processing time of four hours for priority orders. Its automated infrastructure supports the handling of footwear, apparel and accessories while providing flexibility to manage seasonal demand fluctuations. The inauguration also follows the renewal of the partnership between ID Logistics and PUMA for an additional six years. Warehouse automation supports faster order processing The Vendenheim facility incorporates an AutoStore automated storage and retrieval system integrated with the Reflex Warehouse Management System (WMS). The installation includes 15 order-picking stations and 12 product induction stations, with an initial storage capacity of 70,000 bins. The system can be expanded to more than 85,000 bins by 2030 to accommodate potential growth in PUMA’s logistics volumes. ID Logistics manages receiving, storage, order picking, shipping and returns at the site, with processing priorities adjusted according to customer requirements. The facility employs approximately 100 people on average, with staffing levels increasing to 150 during peak periods. Employees from the previous Landersheim operation have transferred to Vendenheim, while additional local recruitment and training have supported the transition. “Ten years after the start of our collaboration with PUMA, the inauguration of Vendenheim marks a new milestone in our partnership,” said Frédéric Grenier, Managing Director of ID Logistics France. Grenier added that the platform was designed to meet supply chain responsiveness requirements while providing capacity for future expansion. Supporting long-term logistics operations The new platform also incorporates environmental features intended to improve its operational sustainability. The facility has achieved BREEAM Excellent certification and includes LED lighting, energy consumption monitoring systems, rooftop photovoltaic generation for self-consumption and electric vehicle charging infrastructure. For PUMA, the investment is intended to strengthen its ability to respond to changing distribution requirements and support the continued development of its French operations. “Logistics performance is a key driver of our development in France. With this new platform, we are strengthening our ability to respond more quickly, better meet the expectations of our business partners and support our long-term growth,” said Christophe Cance, Managing Director, Southern Europe, PUMA. The Vendenheim facility represents a further investment in automated contract logistics, combining warehouse technology with scalable storage capacity to support PUMA’s distribution network in France.

articles.title: China tightens export oversight with new technology and drone controls
articles.summary: China has announced new export control measures covering selected advanced technologies and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), introducing additional compliance requirements for exporters and international logistics providers. The measures, outlined in separate announcements by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) in...
articles.body: China has announced new export control measures covering selected advanced technologies and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), introducing additional compliance requirements for exporters and international logistics providers. The measures, outlined in separate announcements by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) in October 2026, affect technology transfers, export authorizations and customs documentation. While some requirements have already taken effect, further controls are scheduled to become applicable in November, giving businesses different deadlines to assess their export compliance obligations. New requirements for advanced technologies Under Announcement No. 48 of 2026, MOFCOM and the Ministry of Science and Technology proposed adding 40 technologies to China’s Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. The proposed additions cover 23 artificial intelligence-related technologies, five biomedical technologies and 12 photovoltaic technologies. The scope also includes certain core equipment incorporating or utilizing the technologies concerned. The proposed changes remain open for public comment until November 15, 2026. However, an interim export pre-registration requirement took effect when the announcement was published. According to logistics provider Expeditors, this requirement also applies to covered transactions that have already commenced but remain incomplete, including certain shipments in transit. The distinction is important for exporters, as the proposed catalogue amendments are not yet finalized, while the interim registration obligation is already applicable. Additional controls on unmanned aerial vehicles In a separate measure, MOFCOM, the General Administration of Customs and the Central Military Commission Equipment Development Department announced updated export controls covering specified UAVs and related technologies. The controls extend to certain engines, autopilots, communication equipment, motors, propeller blades, flight-control systems and autonomous-navigation technologies. Beginning November 18, 2026, exports of covered items will require authorization under China’s applicable export control framework. Exporters will also need to provide relevant technical information in customs declarations, including for certain products with specifications close to those of controlled items. China’s Dual-Use Items Export Control List will be updated alongside the implementation of the new measures. Implications for international shipments The announcements introduce additional compliance considerations for companies handling technology-related exports from China. Freight forwarders, customs brokers and exporters will need to distinguish between technology transfers subject to interim registration requirements and UAV-related products requiring export authorization from November 18. The measures also underline the importance of accurate product classification and technical documentation, particularly where equipment specifications determine whether export controls apply. For shipments already underway, the interim registration provisions may require additional checks to establish whether a transaction falls within the scope of the new requirements. The announcements do not establish a general prohibition on exports of all AI, biomedical, photovoltaic or drone-related products. Their application depends on the technologies, items and technical specifications covered by the respective measures.

articles.title: Ryder raises full-year outlook as freight market conditions improve
articles.summary: Ryder System reported stronger third-quarter earnings and raised its full-year 2026 profit outlook, supported by improving freight market conditions, higher contractual revenue and continued execution of its strategic initiatives. The US-based logistics and transportation company generated total revenue of $3.43...
articles.body: Ryder System reported stronger third-quarter earnings and raised its full-year 2026 profit outlook, supported by improving freight market conditions, higher contractual revenue and continued execution of its strategic initiatives. The US-based logistics and transportation company generated total revenue of $3.43 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 8% from $3.17 billion a year earlier. Operating revenue, which excludes certain fuel and subcontracted transportation revenue, rose 6% to $2.76 billion. Net earnings increased to $162 million from $138 million, while diluted earnings per share from continuing operations climbed 25% to $4.16. Comparable earnings per share, a non-GAAP measure, rose 21% to $4.33. The company attributed its performance to growth in contractual businesses, improved used vehicle sales and stronger rental operations. Supply chain operations support growth Ryder’s Supply Chain Solutions (SCS) segment recorded third-quarter revenue of $1.50 billion, up 9% year-on-year. Operating revenue also increased 9% to $1.13 billion, supported by new business, higher volumes and improved pricing. However, growth was partially offset by lost business in the automotive sector. Segment earnings before taxes increased 7% to $91 million, reflecting benefits from strategic initiatives and higher operating revenue. Fleet Management Solutions (FMS) generated revenue of $1.62 billion, representing a 10% increase. Earnings before taxes rose 21% to $177 million, supported by contractual business performance, improved rental operations and stronger used vehicle sales. Meanwhile, Dedicated Transportation Solutions (DTS) reported revenue growth of 6% to $606 million. However, operating revenue declined 1% as lower fleet counts offset higher pricing, while segment earnings before taxes decreased 5% to $34 million. “During the quarter, the business benefited from strengthening freight market conditions. Contractual sales activity remained strong across all three segments, with activity accelerating in lease and dedicated,” said John Diez, Chief Executive Officer of Ryder. Ryder increases investment and upgrades outlook The company also announced plans to increase its full-year investment in rental fleet equipment to $500 million, compared with its previous forecast of $300 million. According to Ryder, the additional investment is intended to position the business for higher anticipated rental demand in 2027. The decision follows improving rental fleet utilization, which reached 77% during the third quarter, compared with 70% a year earlier. Ryder raised its full-year 2026 comparable earnings per share forecast to $14.85–$15.05 and increased its adjusted return on equity outlook to 18%–19%. The company maintained its forecast for operating revenue growth of 3% and free cash flow of $700 million to $800 million. Ryder’s updated outlook reflects management’s expectations for continued earnings growth, supported by contractual logistics activities, strategic initiatives and improving conditions in selected freight transportation markets.

MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Prospector 5 jack-up rig Source: Borr Drilling After the Prospector 5 jack-up drilling rig lost stability and sank off the coast of Gabon late Saturday night, triggering an extensive search and rescue operation for the 115 offshore workers on board, 110 personnel have been safely accounted for. Shipments via the Caspian Sea have also risen sharply, with most cargoes destined for Iran. Egypt, once the largest importer of Russian wheat and a key destination for Black Sea shipments, imported 1.35 million tons of Russian grain between July and October, according to ProZerno. Oct 24 (Reuters) – Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after anoffshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighboring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah. The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given. The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE’s northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict’s environmental fallout . Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts’ planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island. The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE’s first commercial gaming license in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027. Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East. Residents reported unusual odors in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE’s environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday. UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. REUTERS/Enea Lebrun By Devon Pendleton and Fabiano Maisonnave Oct 22, 2026 (Bloomberg) –To hedge-fund billionaire Louis Bacon, the crystalline waters and densely forested riverways of the Gulf of Chiriqui in western Panama are an ecological oasis. To developer John McKeown, the gulf is a conduit to potential markets for the region’s prized produce and a boon for its economy. Those clashing visions are at the heart of a bitter dispute between the two wealthy Americans, who both say they’re championing Panama’s best interests. The feud centers on a $260 million port McKeown is seeking to develop on the country’s Pacific coast, just south of the city of David. Ocean Pacific Investments, the company McKeown leads, describes the project, Puerto Baru, as Panama’s first “green” port that will help relieve pressure on trading hubs in Panama City and integrate with trade routes to North America and Asia. Chiriqui, with a population of around 500,000, is Panama’s breadbasket, cultivating foods including coffee, papayas and shrimp. The battle has escalated all the way to Panama’s Supreme Court, which is weighing the port’s environmental approval after a group of local nonprofits challenged it. Already, the fight has involved civil and criminal complaints against some of those NGOs. The outcome will dictate the fate of an unspoiled pocket of Panama that’s seen little of the wealth that flows through its high-flying capital. To Bacon, the project poses an unacceptable risk. “I am concerned that the principals behind this project have no experience developing or operating commercial ports, yet they are proposing a major port in one of the most environmentally sensitive areas in Panama,” he wrote in a statement to Bloomberg News. “A simple look at the map would tell you this is not a suitable development site.” Ocean Pacific, for its part, said that it has addressed potential environmental impacts and that the campaign to stop the port may be motivated by personal interests. “If I believed Puerto Baru would cause significant harm to a part of Panama, a country I not only love but call home, I would never have committed myself or my resources to developing this project,” McKeown said in a statement. The site at issue is nested among the serpentine channels that hold a quarter of Panama’s mangrove forests. Mangrove trees and their dense root systems fortify coastlines, shelter sea life and suck up enormous amounts of carbon . Ocean Pacific envisages a 124-hectare (306-acre) commercial port. It would be the biggest private investment in Chiriqui Province’s history, Ocean Pacific says, and the area would benefit not just from an increase in industry but also more tourism, since there will be a dock for leisure vessels. An economic assessment commissioned by the company in 2021 estimated that the project could create upwards of 1,100 jobs. Six Panamanian environmental groups say the facility, and the resulting cargo-ship traffic, would irreversibly damage the local ecosystem through pollution , water churn and blocked sunlight. Juan Carlos Monterrey Gómez, chief executive officer of environmental consultancy VANGLabs and Panama’s former special representative for climate change, said some impact on the local environment from a project of this size is inevitable. (Monterrey isn’t affiliated with any of the groups opposing it.) A spokesman for Ocean Pacific said the company “strongly disagrees” that the port will cause irreparable damage and said potential impacts were “studied extensively and addressed in detail” as part of the environmental review, which was approved two years ago and was comparable, he said, to reviews conducted for US infrastructure projects. The analysis took four years, according to Ocean Pacific, and included a well-attended public hearing. A website for the project describes it as designed to meet “high sustainability standards,” with solar panels for all its power needs and dedicated conservation zones. The spokesman also said the company has always been clear that it is not a port operator itself, and intends to partner with one. Ocean Pacific has continued to work on the port while the court considers the case. But it struck back at the nonprofits, filing criminal complaints against two of them for slander, libel and crimes against the economy. Shortly afterwards, the two nonprofits said that their bank accounts were frozen due to a court order. Unable to pay staff or raise funds, the groups are struggling to stay afloat and the staff say the measures have spooked other charities that might otherwise be speaking out. The case is producing the kind of chill associated with so-called SLAPP lawsuits, which are meant to intimidate critics, said Joana Abrego, former legal manager and now an external consultant for CIAM, one of the affected groups. Ocean Pacific declined to comment on ongoing litigation. One reason that CIAM and the other accused nonprofit, Adopta Bosque, were able to voice such strong opposition in the first place is Louis Bacon. The 70-year-old financier made a fortune through his hedge fund Moore Capital Management and has poured some of it into land and various conservation efforts around the world. He’s the 70th-biggest landowner in the US, according to the Land Report , and has placed 94% of that land under conservation easements, a legal tool that permanently bans future development. The term conservationist suggests quiet stewardship, but that’s not Bacon’s style. He co-founded Waterkeeper Alliance, a nonprofit formerly run by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that aims to enforce environmental laws. Through his nonprofit, the Moore Charitable Foundation, he has often taken an activist approach, collaborating with local advocacy groups to oppose projects near his properties, such as a cement plant in North Carolina. He notably was involved in a bitter yearslong feud with Peter Nygard, the disgraced Canadian fashion mogul, that was tied to their neighboring properties in the Bahamas. The fight over Baru, too, is personal. Bacon owns Islas Secas, an all-inclusive eco-tourism resort that sits on an archipelago about 30 miles southwest of the proposed port, and where nightly rates start at $3,500. He said the port, if built, is far away enough that it won’t directly affect his island, but the dredging and habitat disruption would have cascading consequences. He’s not fighting the project to defend his luxury hotel, he said, and his commitment to Panama won’t change even if the port goes ahead. Bacon described Ocean Pacific’s legal action against the nonprofits as extraordinary. “I’ve never had to support environmental advocates facing criminal penalties simply for raising concerns about a development project,” he said. “Lawfare against whistleblowers is abominable.” Bacon has personally covered Adopta Bosque’s legal costs and also helped fund the broader campaign against the project, which includes an online petition and a website articulating the six nonprofits’ mission, endorsed by nearly four dozen “supportive organizations,” many of which Bacon has funded in the past for their wider work. He paid for an alternative port plan that endorsed moving it about 50 miles west to the city of Puerto Armuelles, and his foundation funded an impact analysis that estimated the port’s environmental toll would come to around $30 million over 20 years. McKeown also has personal ties to Panama. A part-time resident of the country, he said he first became interested in Chiriqui’s potential as a maritime hub while on a deep-sea fishing excursion; the captain had to travel seven hours to resupply because there was no suitable dock. He has experience bridging enterprise and conservation efforts. As president of the closely-held Los Angeles-area energy company, Synergy Oil & Gas, he helped create one of California’s biggest protected wetlands with authorities by agreeing to decommission what had been an active oil field. Before Synergy, McKeown was a real estate broker and owned several container and logistics yards. He said he’s raised money for Puerto Baru from various US individuals, whom he declined to identify. Bacon said he’s expressed his concerns about the project with Panamanian officials personally and through his local foundation, and that he reached out to Ocean Pacific with an offer to help pay for additional scientific analyses and a coastal modeling study but didn’t get a response. An Ocean Pacific spokesman said McKeown exchanged emails with Bacon’s son Trevor and concluded that new analyses would duplicate work that had already been done. McKeown said Puerto Armuelles was too far from the region’s farms to be feasible. Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said in a statement that the ministry is legally “obliged to respect” the environmental approval for Puerto Baru — which a previous administration signed off on — and that it will abide by the Supreme Court’s decision when it comes. He declined to comment on Ocean Pacific’s lawsuits against the NGOs but said the nature of the suits had ministry officials “deeply concerned.” “Panama is a democratic country,” he said. “At the Ministry of Environment we value and promote active, robust citizen participation, as well as contributions from civil society and the scientific community to environmental management.” Panamanian advocates say the port project exposes what they describe as a chasm between Panama’s reputation as a leader on conservation and the environment and its treatment of local nonprofits. “Organizations like ours are on our own. We don’t have institutions that protect us in this situation,” said Abrego. Two environmentalists opposing Puerto Baru declined to speak on the record out of fear for their safety criticizing the state’s stance on a development project. The dissonance isn’t that unusual, said Monterrey, the former climate envoy, given the knotty bureaucratic interests that complicate most countries’ policies. In his view, the port likely wouldn’t deliver what its developers are promising for Panama. “These large projects are usually presented as bringing jobs and development,” he said, “but they often produce social conflict, extract wealth from the communities and send the returns elsewhere.” Whether Ocean Pacific gets the chance to change that narrative is now up to the high court. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure,...

Join the leading maritime news network Image credit: NOAA Fisheries The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure, and tougher enforcement against unfair foreign competition. The strategy , announced October 23, builds on President Donald Trump’s April 2025 executive order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness , and brings together several federal agencies to expand domestic seafood production, modernize processing capacity, and improve market access for American fishermen. A major focus is rebuilding the infrastructure that supports the nation’s commercial fishing fleet, including shipyards, docks, cold storage facilities, processing plants, and working waterfronts. Federal agencies will work to streamline permitting and reduce barriers to private investment, while making greater use of existing financing programs administered by NOAA, the Department of Agriculture, and the Small Business Administration. NOAA will also review its Fisheries Finance Program and Capital Construction Fund to identify obstacles that discourage fishermen from replacing aging vessels or investing in safer, more efficient American-built fishing boats. “The America First Seafood Strategy ensures that the future of seafood in the United States will be built by American fishermen, American workers, and American industry—not by foreign imports,” said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The initiative comes as the administration pursues a broader effort to rebuild America’s maritime industrial base, including domestic shipbuilding capacity and the U.S.-flagged fleet. Beyond infrastructure, the strategy calls for changes to federal fisheries management aimed at increasing sustainable harvests and reducing regulatory costs. NOAA will work with regional fishery management councils and industry representatives to ensure catch limits reflect the best available science, restore access to productive fishing grounds where supported by data, and eliminate compliance requirements that do not contribute to conservation goals. The administration also plans to strengthen the position of American seafood in domestic markets. A proposed voluntary “U.S.-Caught Seafood” designation would help consumers identify products harvested by American fishermen aboard U.S.-flagged vessels operating under U.S. fisheries management. The Food and Drug Administration issued draft guidance Friday outlining how companies could use U.S.-origin statements and labeling. Federal agencies will also seek to expand purchases of American seafood through government procurement programs and launch a nationwide “Eat American Seafood” campaign. On the trade front, the strategy calls for stronger enforcement against illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, seafood fraud, and mislabeling. NOAA plans to improve its Seafood Import Monitoring Program, using advanced technology and more targeted inspections to identify high-risk imports. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative will also work with other agencies to address unfair foreign trade practices and improve access to overseas markets for American seafood exporters. Marine aquaculture is another priority, with federal agencies expected to establish clearer permitting standards for operations in federal waters. Notably, the strategy does not announce new federal spending. Instead, it relies on existing programs and statutory authorities, with an emphasis on regulatory changes, interagency coordination, and attracting private investment. NOAA said progress will be measured through increases in domestic seafood production and processing, private capital investment, American jobs supported, and reduced dependence on foreign supply chains. The broader goal is to keep more of the economic value of American seafood in the United States, from vessels harvesting fish offshore to the shipyards, processors, and waterfront businesses that support the industry. Photo courtesy Philly Shipyard By Ira Breskin BRONX, NY — Vessel Construction Management practices received praise at the Shipbuilding in America conference here this week. Vessel Construction Management (VCM) essentially outsources oversight of a ship’s entire construction process, from design to delivery, to a third party acting as the owner’s representative. The vessel construction manager takes charge of the entire project, from procuring materials to testing the vessel before delivery. The Maritime Administration (MARAD) recently embraced VCM when procuring a new generation of training ships for five of the six state maritime academies. To date, MARAD contractor TOTE Services has delivered four of the five vessels. “The goal is to deliver a newbuild ship on time and on budget by reducing direct government involvement with the yard and making the construction process more commercial than normal government procurement,” said Charlie Papavizas, an attorney with Winston Taylor in Washington, D.C. The next challenge is to expand the use of VCM in commercial shipbuilding, said Chris Clark, vice president of new construction at TOTE Services, during the conference. The conference was held earlier this week at the State University of New York Maritime College. Empire State VII, the school’s new training ship, was the first in the series to be delivered on time and within budget by TOTE, arriving in September 2023. TOTE Services is also using VCM practices in two subsequent government projects: the construction of missile range instrumentation vessels and a new class of medium landing ships for the Navy. Several ship operators and ship management companies offer VCM services, with the scope of those services depending on each firm’s expertise. VCM relies on commercial shipbuilding best practices and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components rather than military-specification parts, both of which can reduce vessel costs and speed delivery. Moreover, the use of VCM minimizes unnecessary design changes and the resulting change orders, which are often a source of costly contract disputes. articles.title: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan
articles.summary: China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines.Responding…
articles.body: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Copyright TomKorcak/AdobeStock China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines. Responding to a Reuters exclusive this month on the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat off Taiwan's Pacific coast in mid-August, the coast guard said it had dispatched a patrol boat to drive away the vessel, which was operating alongside a Chinese coast guard ship and a research vessel. The coast guard confirmed details in the Reuters report, identifying the suspected militia fishing boat as Minfudingyu 07902 , and said it had come as close as about 2.7 nautical miles outside Taiwan's restricted waters on August 16. China has increased such activity since June in overlapping economic waters involving Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, the coast guard said, after Tokyo and Manila announced talks on maritime boundary delimitation in their exclusive economic zones. EEZs extend 200 nautical miles from the coast and give a coastal state rights to exploit, conserve and manage natural resources in those waters. "Such complex grey-zone operations not only increase the maritime surveillance and response burden on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, but may also create regional security pressure and affect the existing international maritime order," Taiwan's Coast Guard said in a statement to Reuters. China's defence ministry, and the Philippines defence and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Japan's coast guard declined immediate comment. The coast guard said the vessels' coordinated activity was part of a broader pattern of Chinese "grey-zone" operations using law-enforcement, scientific and civilian cover to expand Beijing's influence at sea while remaining below the threshold of open conflict. The Chinese operations were aimed at "assisting 'battlefield preparation'," the coast guard said, adding Taiwan's east coast was an important maritime traffic and supply route and that continued Chinese activity there could further increase security pressure on Taiwan. Officials in Taiwan say they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve its goals. Taiwan's government rejects the claim and says only the island's people can decide their future. China has repeatedly said its operations off Taiwan's east coast are "legitimate and lawful" because they are in Chinese waters, a position Taipei's government strongly rejects. Taiwan's coast guard said it had placed the Minfudingyu 07902 on a priority watchlist, assessing the boat showed the "characteristics" of Chinese maritime militia activity and said it would continue tracking the vessel. Dating back to the 1950s, China's maritime militia uses fishing vessels with trained, state-supported crews to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships around South China Sea flashpoints, helping Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance. The surveillance report reviewed by Reuters was conducted by Taiwan's Apex Aviation, which used radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data from a reconnaissance flight to document the cluster of vessels.
