The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. The extension would provide another reprieve for shipping companies facing potentially significant fees on Chinese-owned, Chinese-operated and Chinese-built vessels calling at U.S. ports, as well as certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. “The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation,” USTR said in the notice. Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. During that period, shipping companies would not incur liability for port fees under Annexes I, II and III of the original Section 301 action. The suspension would also continue to cover certain duties on ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment. The proposed extension comes nearly a year after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to suspend the port fees as part of a broader trade agreement reached in South Korea. Washington began collecting the fees on October 14, 2025, but suspended them on November 10, meaning the measures were in effect for less than four weeks. China also suspended its retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. The original measures emerged from a Section 301 investigation launched during the Biden administration following a 2024 petition by the United Steelworkers and other labor organizations. The investigation concluded that China’s industrial policies and subsidies distorted global competition and undermined U.S. commerce. The resulting port fees became a central part of the Trump administration’s strategy to counter China’s maritime dominance and encourage investment in American shipbuilding. Growing Pressure to Reinstate Fees The latest proposal comes despite mounting pressure from some lawmakers and maritime labor groups to bring the fees back. In June, Senators Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) urged the administration to immediately reinstate the measures , arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild the U.S. commercial shipbuilding industry. “Section 301 port fees are critical to revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding,” the senators wrote in a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The lawmakers pointed to China’s growing share of global shipbuilding, noting that Chinese yards now account for more than half of global commercial vessel production, compared with just 0.1% for the United States. They also questioned whether Washington had secured meaningful concessions from Beijing in exchange for suspending the fees and how the administration intended to fund its proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund without the revenue. Maritime labor unions have similarly criticized the suspension, arguing that it weakens one of the few measures specifically designed to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry. Shipping companies, meanwhile, have welcomed the reprieve. The original fees threatened to impose substantial costs on carriers and disrupt established shipping networks. During the brief period the measures were active, U.S. carrier Matson reported incurring $6.4 million in reciprocal Chinese port fees, while China’s state-owned COSCO faced an estimated $1.5 billion in annual U.S. charges. Andy Abbott, CEO of ACL, told gCaptain that any port fees would impact its growing US export business, and customers are concerned ACL. “ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” explained Abbott. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade. This development allows us to continue serving the US market with the fastest transit times from the US East Coast to Europe.” The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and World Shipping Council both welcomed last year’s suspension, warning that the competing U.S. and Chinese measures risked increasing transportation costs and disrupting global trade. A Broader Debate Over Port Fees The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year. Unlike the China-specific Section 301 measures, the plan envisions fees on all foreign-built commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports, with proceeds supporting domestic shipbuilding through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund. The plan outlined potential fees ranging from 1 cent to 25 cents per kilogram of imported cargo, which the administration estimated could generate as much as $1.5 trillion over 10 years at the upper end. ICS has warned that such broad-based charges could significantly increase shipping costs and disrupt global trade, even as it supports efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity. The proposals underscore the competing pressures facing the administration as it seeks to revive American shipyards without imposing additional costs on U.S. importers, exporters and consumers. For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue. USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Eastern Time on October 30. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694. The extension has not yet been finalized. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. articles.title: Brent Crude Prices Reach Five-Month High Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks, UAE Oil Spill

articles.body: Brent Crude Prices Reach Five-Month High Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks, UAE Oil Spill Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Аня Крамарова Oil prices rose on Friday, with Brent crude touching its highest since early May, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill . Brent crude futures gained $1.71, or 1.5%, to $114.99 a barrel by 1300 GMT, having earlier reached $115.16, the highest level since May 4. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.80, or 1.8%, to $101.27. The Brent benchmark is on track for a 4.4% weekly rise, its third in a row, while WTI is poised to finish 0.4% down on the week. Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis. An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved. Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. "The market remains concerned about a potential escalation, which, in a worst-case scenario, could trigger renewed supply disruptions," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo, adding that volatile oil flows and elevated freight rates have left the market undersupplied. Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday. Meanwhile, the first Russian diesel bound for the US since an export agreement between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday. Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3. (Reuters)

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October
articles.summary: October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017."October…
articles.body: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/S.Gvozd October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. "October has seen the highest number of ship attacks on record," said Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Raydan, who maintains the institute's interactive shipping incident map, has recorded 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The institute's map shows most of the attacks that took place in September and October were in the Strait of Hormuz. AROUND 3.5% OF WORLD SUPERTANKER FLEET ATTACKED The tally broadly aligns with data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), which recorded a total of 120 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict with Iran began. The IMO lists more than 30 supertankers, or Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), that were damaged during the attacks, including 11 in October alone, a Reuters review of the IMO list and MarineTraffic vessel data showed. Each VLCC can carry about 2 million barrels of crude. The listed vessels account for about 3.5% of the total global VLCC fleet, which exceeds 900. More tankers came under attack as shipowners became increasingly willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf, lured by daily freight rates exceeding $1 million and steeper discounts offered by regional producers against dated Brent. "October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March," Greece-based consultancy Marisks said. Between October 5 and October 11, a dozen ships were attacked, marking also the highest weekly number of attacks since the conflict began, it also said. NOT ALL ATTACKS MAY BE CAPTURED IN DATA By intensifying attacks, Iran is seeking to slow the recovery in shipments and maintain pressure on global energy markets ahead of November's US midterm elections, Raydan said. Earlier this month, Reuters reported about Tehran adopting such tactics, citing two senior Iranian officials. UKMTO, the British maritime security service, which recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran conflict as of October 16, said it was struggling to capture the whole picture due to insufficient voluntary reporting by shippers. The UKMTO data also showed a sharp rise in ship damage caused by attacks in October. articles.summary: Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S.
articles.body: U.S. Navy Secretary Visits Fincantieri Wisconsin Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao visits Fincantieri shipyard in Wisconsin. Image courtesy Fincantieri Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S. Navy's Landing Ship Medium (LSM) vessels . The delegation included Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Maritime Administration Administrator Stephen Carmel, OMB Associate Director for Shipbuilding Jerry Hendrix and Eugenio Santagata , General Manager of Fincantieri's Naval Vessels Division. George Moutafis, CEO of Fincantieri Marine Group, and Jan Allman, CEO of Fincantieri Marinette Marine, outlined the company's shipbuilding programs, capital investments and efforts to accelerate production. At Marinette, officials toured the automated panel production line and observed demonstrations of collaborative robots, augmented and virtual reality tools, and powered air-purifying respirators. Fincantieri is integrating these technologies to improve production efficiency and worker safety. At Sturgeon Bay, the delegation reviewed the shipyard's capabilities and its role in supporting simultaneous construction of multiple vessel classes. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize" is not part of this release; instead, Moutafis emphasized the company's investments in workforce capabilities and advanced technologies to increase production rates and meet Navy requirements. The visit comes as Fincantieri Marinette Marine prepares to begin construction of four LSM vessels for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, subject to negotiations with program manager TOTE Services. In April, the Navy awarded Fincantieri an initial $30 million contract for procurement of critical materials associated with the LSM program. "Our Navy needs more skilled professionals like those I had the opportunity to meet today in order to remain the strongest Navy in the world," Cao said. The Wisconsin facilities are positioned to serve as the industrial center for Fincantieri's LSM work, expanding their role in the U.S. naval shipbuilding industrial base. articles.body: 18th Tug Delivered by Sanmar Shipyards to SAAM Towage Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Sanmar Shipyards Sanmar Shipyards has delivered SAAM XIMBAL, a new BOGAÇAY Class tug, to SAAM Towage, marking the 18th SANMAR-built tug delivered to the towage operator since 2018. Known as BOGAÇAY XCVI during construction in Türkiye, SAAM XIMBAL will operate from the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas on Mexico's Pacific coast, supporting demanding ship-handling operations at one of the country's major commercial ports. SAAM XIMBAL is based on the RAmparts 2400SX-MK|I design, developed exclusively for SANMAR by Canadian naval architects Robert Allan Ltd. The latest delivery brings the number of BOGAÇAY Class tugs in the SAAM Towage fleet to 13. Powered by two CAT 3516E main engines, each producing 2,350 KW at 1,800 rpm, SAAM XIMBAL combines high performance with environmentally responsible operation. A high level of onboard automation supports operational efficiency, while a sewage treatment unit and oily water separator further reduce the vessel's environmental impact as per SAAM sustainability requisites With an overall length of 24.4 meters, a molded beam of 12 meters, a least moulded depth of 4.5 meters and a navigational draught of 5.45 meters, SAAM XIMBAL combines compact dimensions with the power required for demanding harbor operations. The tug delivers over 80 tonnes of bollard pull and achieves a free-running speed of 13 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi 1 firefighting capability, further enhancing its operational versatility. SAAM XIMBAL joins a diverse group of SANMAR-built vessels already operating in the SAAM Towage fleet. Alongside the 13 BOGAÇAY Class tugs, these include three all-electric ElectRA harbor tugs and two powerful BIGAÇAY Class RAstar 29005X tugs.

The FSO PTSC Lac Da Vang (FSO PTSC LDV) has reached its first oil operational milestone at the Lac Da Vang field in Block 15-1/05 offshore Vietnam on September 27, 2026, ahead of the previously communicated Q4 2026 schedule. The FSO features a storage capacity of 460,000 barrels and is designed to enhance operational efficiency while supporting sustainable offshore oilfield operations. The FSO PTSC LDV is chartered to Murphy Cuu Long Bac Oil, a wholly owned subsidiary of Murphy Oil Corporation, under a ten-year firm contract with extension options of up to five additional years. The field's development is expected to ramp up through 2028 as additional wells are brought online, providing a vital new source of production to support Vietnam’s growing energy sector. Murphy Oil is the operator of Block 15-1/05 of the Cuu Long Basin with a 40% working interest, while its partners, PetroVietnam Exploration Production and SK Earthon, hold the remaining 35% and 25%, respectively. (ACI) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance plans for a floating dry dock and marine repair facility at the Port of Argentia in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. The proposed development would combine Mammoet's heavy lifting, transport and marine engineering capabilities with the port's existing infrastructure, creating additional capacity for vessel maintenance, repair and industrial services. Central to the project is the Tugdock Submersible Platform (TSP) , developed by Mammoet subsidiary Tugdock Submersible Platforms Ltd. The modular floating dry dock system is designed to accommodate vessels of varying sizes and can be scaled to meet changing operational requirements, providing an alternative to conventional fixed dry dock infrastructure. The proposed facility would also leverage Argentia's existing graving dock, deepwater, ice-free harbor and extensive industrial property to support year-round operations. "This partnership represents an exciting opportunity to build on Mammoet's established presence at Argentia and introduce advanced, scalable marine technology to the Canadian market," said Jeremy Asher, Managing Director at Mammoet. The partners envision a multi-client facility serving commercial shipping, offshore oil and gas, offshore wind, the Canadian Coast Guard and the Royal Canadian Navy. Mammoet already operates at Argentia, including work associated with the former Cenovus Graving Dock site and offshore wind marshalling projects. Scott Penney, CEO of Port of Argentia, said the agreement builds on the port's existing relationship with Mammoet and opportunities emerging across Canada's marine industry. The partners will next initiate a formal Expression of Interest process to identify an experienced international marine industrial operator capable of managing the proposed facility. The MOU represents an initial development step, with the partners seeking to establish a competitive marine repair operation while expanding Newfoundland and Labrador's industrial capacity and creating opportunities for regional suppliers and skilled trades.

articles.summary: The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has launched Ocean Minerals Forward, a new industry education and communications initiative examining the potential of deep-sea mineral resources to strengthen U.S. critical mineral supply chains…
articles.body: NOIA Launches Ocean Minerals Initiative Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Courtesy NOIA The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has launched Ocean Minerals Forward, a new industry education and communications initiative examining the potential of deep-sea mineral resources to strengthen U.S. critical mineral supply chains, support domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The initiative includes a dedicated website, a comprehensive report and educational resources covering seabed mineral development, offshore technologies, environmental considerations and the regulatory challenges facing the emerging industry. Critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese and rare earth elements are increasingly important to defense systems, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure and digital technologies. With global processing and refining capacity concentrated in a limited number of countries, NOIA argues that ocean mineral resources could complement terrestrial mining, recycling and imports from allied nations. “America cannot afford to remain dependent on foreign-controlled supply chains for the minerals that power our economy and national defense,” said NOIA President Erik Milito. “The ocean holds significant mineral resources, and companies across the U.S. and allied nations are bringing the technology, offshore expertise, and investment needed to unlock their potential.” A central theme of the initiative is the potential application of existing offshore oil and gas industry capabilities to seabed mineral exploration and recovery. Click here to download the full report. NOIA points to decades of experience in deepwater operations, including subsea robotics, autonomous underwater vehicles, geophysical surveying, dynamic positioning, specialized offshore vessels and environmental monitoring. These technologies could provide a foundation for future ocean mineral projects while creating opportunities for U.S. shipyards, ports, subsea contractors and equipment manufacturers. Environmental considerations are also addressed, including the potential effects of sediment plumes, impacts on deep-sea biodiversity and the need for environmental assessments, monitoring and regulatory oversight. The Ocean Minerals Forward report examines resource potential, global supply chain concentration, China's role in mineral processing, emerging collection technologies and opportunities for American offshore companies. NOIA said it plans to expand the platform with additional research, industry case studies and updates as technology, regulation and commercial opportunities develop. The initiative comes as the offshore industry evaluates the technical, environmental and economic feasibility of commercial seabed mineral recovery, an emerging sector where significant questions remain about environmental impacts, permitting and the development of viable processing and supply chains.

articles.title: Natural gas discovery springs up in India’s shallow waters
articles.summary: Oil India has found natural gas in the Krishna-Godavari Basin's shallow waters, augmenting India’s hydrocarbon arsenal.
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 23, 2026 · 2 days ago Natural gas discovery springs up in India’s shallow waters Oil India has found natural gas in the Krishna-Godavari Basin's shallow waters, augmenting India’s hydrocarbon arsenal. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Oil India Oil India Limited (OIL), an exploration and production company, has increased its offshore reserves with a new natural gas discovery in the previously unappraised Matsyapuri formation of the Krishna-Godavari Basin. Drilled as an appraisal well in the shallow offshore block KG-DSF/GSKW/2018, the Godavari-1 well yielded strong gas flows reaching up to 2 lakh standard cubic meters per day (scumd) alongside condensate, marking a promising new milestone for the Maharatna CPSE's hydrocarbon portfolio. articles.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Operations Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 1,515 2 minutes read Bocimar Bocimar Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. The mining group said the port expansion would improve shipping efficiency and reduce freight costs, strengthening its ability to supply overseas customers and Australian alumina refineries. Despite the larger vessels and additional mining capacity, analysts at SEB see limited upside for the capesize market from the investment. The bank noted that much of the new production will replace output from existing mines, leaving a relatively modest increase of around 6m tonnes compared with current Weipa production levels. Any additional volumes are also several years away. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand. The bank argued that additional Australian volumes could therefore work against the shift towards longer-haul Guinea-China trades, with the overall impact on dry bulk shipping likely to be negligible. Construction at Kangwinan is scheduled to accelerate in 2027, with the investment including $150m already approved for early works last year. The latest commitment follows Rio Tinto’s September agreement to acquire the neighbouring Aurukun bauxite project from Glencore and Mitsubishi, subject to regulatory approvals. The company intends to integrate the deposit into its longer-term development plans for the region, using existing and planned infrastructure. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. PTTEP MENA, PTTEP’s wholly owned subsidiary, together with Eni Abu Dhabi, has established Seela Energies, with each company holding a 50% shareholding. Each of the founders holds a 10% participating interest in the Ghasha concession project , which will now be transferred to the newly formed JV. This concession is considered to be one of the world's largest sulfur-rich gas development projects and a cornerstone of the UAE's strategy to achieve gas self-sufficiency and support rising international export demand. The development concept encompasses multiple fields, including Hail and Ghasha , located in shallow waters. This project utilizes a series of artificial islands rather than traditional platforms to drill and manage operations while minimizing environmental disturbance. ADNOC’s partners in the Ghasha concession, aside from Eni and PTTEP, which consolidated their joint stakes under Seela Energies, involved other companies across the broader project lifecycle, including Wintershall Dea, OMV, and Lukoil. The Ghasha development is envisioned to employ smart technology across all operations, allowing operators, technicians, and site personnel remote access to the project’s operations. Aside from a fully unmanned facility, ADNOC has set its sights on artificial intelligence (AI), such as predictive maintenance, for all critical rotating equipment. A few months ago, the operator, in partnership with Eni and PTTEP, put into place a structured financing transaction of up to $11 billion (AED 40.4 billion) for Hail and Ghasha sour gas development. The UAE giant’s financing model follows a series of midstream and infrastructure transactions, including a $4.9 billion (AED 18 billion) oil pipeline partnership and a $10.1 billion (AED 37.1 billion) gas pipeline agreement. It also comes after build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) projects, such as the $3.8 billion (AED 14 billion) project to power and decarbonize offshore operations and the $2.2 billion (AED 8.3 billion) project to deliver sustainable water supplies to onshore operations. articles.title: Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data
articles.summary: Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 907 1 minute read Britannia P&I Britannia P&I Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to Risk report, published yesterday, examines 68 sources spanning accident investigations, insurance claims, academic studies and seafarer surveys. It finds consistent links between crew wellbeing and safety outcomes, particularly involving fatigue, mental health and psychological safety. Fatigue emerges as the most extensively documented risk factor. The report warns that understaffing and excessive workloads encourage the falsification of rest-hour records, concealing dangerous working conditions from compliance systems. Between a quarter and a third of seafarers do not feel safe raising concerns or reporting mistakes, potentially undermining the accuracy of incident and near-miss reporting. The findings reinforce earlier research covered by Splash . A World Maritime University study published in 2024 found 64.3% of surveyed seafarers adjusted their work/rest records. Another welfare review, reported by Splash last month, found just 49% of seafarers believed their most recent vessel carried sufficient crew to work safely without excessive fatigue. Insurance claims provide further evidence of the financial implications. Gard’s latest crew claims report identifies stress, fatigue and excessive workloads as important factors in onboard injuries, while illness accounts for almost 60% of crew claims. SSI argues insurers can already incorporate welfare indicators into loss-prevention programmes and underwriting discussions, while lenders could include them in borrower monitoring. However, the organisation cautions that current evidence remains insufficient to use welfare indicators as standalone predictors of future claims, insurance premiums or investment performance. The next challenge is connecting existing welfare surveys, accident investigations, port state control findings and insurance claims at vessel and operator level, allowing the industry to quantify how poor crew conditions translate into financial losses. The incident occurred when the ship deviated from its planned course because the second officer on watch fell asleep. Legislation provides the national carrier with rights covering 40% of the value of the country’s import and export cargoes. SLOSCO is headed by chief executive Sui Xiao, with former BRS Shipbrokers executive Laurent Debart serving as chief operating officer. The company has established operations in Freetown, Shanghai and Geneva. The venture represents another expansion of Chinese shipping interests in West Africa, with Freetown seeking to retain more of the freight revenue generated by its international trade. articles.body: Surveys & Interventions October 23, 2026 · 2 days ago Malaysian survey services firm enters collaboration in Indonesia and Timor-Leste NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Helms Geomarine Malaysian offshore soil investigation and geotechnical engineering services company Helms Geomarine has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Indonesia's PT Elnusa Trans Samudera (ENTS) to jointly pursue offshore geotechnical investigation opportunities in Indonesia and Timor-Leste. The collaboration is said to combine HELMS’ specialist geotechnical expertise and drilling resources with ENTS’ marine capabilities, local market knowledge and logistics support. The proposed scope includes offshore geotechnical drilling, soil and rock sampling, seabed testing, laboratory testing and engineering reporting, supported by vessel preparation and mobilization. In addition to individual projects, the collaboration includes plans for establishing a local Helms entity to own strategic drilling resources, using Indonesian-flagged DP2 vessels, employing Indonesian personnel and developing a local laboratory, with technical training and knowledge sharing to strengthen local expertise. articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Europe Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 382 1 minute read Icon Energy Icon Energy Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. Hampton, led by chairman and chief executive Peter Deeb, claims Icon has raised approximately $25m through common share issuances since its 2024 flotation, while ordinary shareholders have suffered substantial losses. The Canadian investment firm has also questioned the treatment of preferred shares held by Icon’s controlling shareholder and chief executive, Ismini Panagiotidi. Hampton is proposing that Icon exchange its outstanding Series A preferred shares for a new instrument with a $20m face value, a fixed 6% cash dividend and conversion rights priced at $5 per ordinary share. It also wants a one-for-one share dividend for existing ordinary shareholders and the appointment of a Hampton-nominated director. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. The proposals have not been accepted or implemented, and the filing does not establish that legal proceedings have commenced. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers. The company entered the Nasdaq market in July 2024 and subsequently expanded its fleet through secondhand acquisitions. Its most recent disclosed commercial moves include fixing the 63,668 dwt ultramax Charlie on an index-linked charter extending into 2027 and acquiring a minority investment in two containership projects. The feeder investment, disclosed in June, marked Icon’s first publicly announced move beyond dry bulk shipping.
